content: Castoreum is the term used to describe the exudate secreted from the castor sacs of mature North American beavers (Castor canadensis) and European beavers (Castor fiber). This substance is a yellowish secretion produced by the castor sacs, which is mixed with the beaver's urine and utilized for scent marking their territory. Both male and female beavers possess a pair of castor sacs and a pair of anal glands, which are located in two cavities beneath the skin between the pelvis and the base of the tail. It is important to note that castor sacs are not true glands, either endocrine or exocrine, at the cellular level. Therefore, referring to these structures as preputial glands or castor glands is a misnomer. In modern times, castoreum is used in trapping, as a tincture in certain perfumes, and is sometimes promoted as an aphrodisiac. The dried castor sacs of beavers are typically aged for two or more years to reduce their raw harshness and develop a more mellow character. In perfumery, castoreum has historically been employed as an animalic note, often evoking a leathery scent. It is blended with other ingredients, including top, middle, and base notes, to create complex compositions. Some classic perfumes that incorporate castoreum include Emeraude, Coty Chanel Cuir de Russie, Magie Noire, Lancôme Caractère, Hechter Madame, Carven, Givenchy III, Shalimar, and various leather-themed fragrances. Chemical analysis of castoreum has identified 24 compounds that contribute to its composition, some of which have been individually screened for pheromonal activity. These include phenols such as 4-ethylphenol and 1,2-dihydroxybenzene, as well as ketones like acetophenone and 3-hydroxyacetophenone. Additional compounds identified include 4-methyl-1,2-dihydroxybenzene, 4-methoxyacetophenone, 5-methoxysalicylic acid, salicylaldehyde, and 3-hydroxybenzoic acid. Medicinal Use of Castoreum Although the modern medical use of castoreum is rare, the dried pair of scent glands (referred to as castors) were historically considered valuable, sometimes even more so than a beaver pelt. Castoreum was included in the materia medica until the 1700s and was used to treat a variety of ailments, including headaches, fevers, and hysteria. The Romans believed that the fumes produced by burning castoreum could induce abortion. Paracelsus, a prominent figure in early medicine, suggested its use in the treatment of epilepsy. Additionally, medieval beekeepers used castoreum to enhance honey production. Castoreum, as an anal gland secretion, appears to play a role in territorial marking behavior among beavers. In small quantities, it has also been used to contribute to the flavor and aroma of cigarettes.
